title: When Contracts Are No Longer Enough
author: Colin Gautrey
summary: Colin Gautrey observes from his September research that organisations are rethinking how they secure the resources they depend on. A contract gives enforceable rights but not necessarily access to what you need when you need it, particularly when suppliers fail, geopolitics intervenes or demand outruns capacity. He cites GE Aerospace moving to acquire a critical casting supplier, Nscale building its own energy and power division, and Google making long-term commitments that support new generating capacity. The common pattern is a deliberate reassessment of how much control is actually needed and in what form, since outright ownership carries costs, obligations and vulnerabilities of its own. He then turns the question to individuals, who depend on systems, institutions and relationships they do not control, and some of whose dependencies exist only because they have never been examined. The post is short and works as a prompt, ending with the question of what you depend on that you cannot afford to lose.
points: Gautrey's core distinction is between enforceable rights under a contract and actual access to a resource when it is scarce, which explains why supply risk now triggers acquisitions and direct investment.
The three examples, GE Aerospace, Nscale and Google, show different responses (buying, building, long-term financing) to the same dependency problem.
He cautions that ownership is not automatically the answer, so the useful question is how much control is needed and what form it should take.
He applies the logic to individual professionals, whose positions, finances and judgement depend on decisions made elsewhere.
Some dependencies are unavoidable but others persist only because nobody questioned them.
quotes: A contract may give you enforceable rights. It does not necessarily give you access to what you need, when you need it.

GE Aerospace moved to acquire a critical casting supplier. Nscale established its own Energy and Power division. Google has gone beyond conventional electricity purchasing, making long-term commitments that help secure the development and continued operation of generating capacity.

The emerging pattern is a deliberate reassessment of control. Organisations are reconsidering whether traditional commercial relationships provide sufficient assurance over the capabilities, resources and infrastructure on which they depend.
And ownership is not necessarily the answer. It brings its own costs, obligations and vulnerabilities.
Our positions, financial arrangements, access to technology and ability to exercise independent judgement can depend on decisions made elsewhere.
Some dependencies are unavoidable. Others exist because we have never seriously questioned them. What do you depend on that you cannot afford to lose?
